name: Planting and germination
process: Set establishment and sprouting are being observed. Timing varies with planting material, temperature, moisture, soil, and method.
observations: Record missing or delayed emergence by a consistent row or area
Check soil moisture and standing water
Inspect setts and young shoots for damage
frequency: Weekly scouting; record an observation when conditions change or a measurement is taken.

activities.title: Walk a fixed section of rows and note emergence gaps
activities.why: A consistent area makes later establishment observations comparable.

activities.title: Check moisture and drainage near the setts
activities.why: Both dry soil and standing water can affect establishment; use local soil and weather advice.

activities.title: Inspect for early weed competition
activities.why: Early weeds can compete with young cane; follow locally registered weed guidance.

name: Early growth and tillering
process: Young shoots and early tillers develop. Actual timing and density depend on variety and field conditions.
observations: Count shoots in a marked area and record its area
Note leaf colour and new leaf development
Check moisture, weed competition, and gaps
frequency: Weekly scouting; count tillers only when using the same marked area and method.

activities.title: Repeat the marked-area shoot count
activities.why: A consistent method helps distinguish a trend from sampling differences.

activities.title: Inspect and record weed pressure
activities.why: Competition can slow early crop development.

activities.title: Review irrigation delivery and recent rainfall
activities.why: This gives context before changing irrigation.

name: Tillering and early canopy
process: Tillering and leaf canopy development continue; do not compare against a numeric target unless a suitable local variety reference is available.
observations: Repeat shoot count with the same area and method
Record visible leaf symptoms and their spread
Inspect drainage, weeds, and crop uniformity
frequency: Weekly scouting; record measured values when collected.

activities.title: Compare the marked-area tiller count with the last count
activities.why: The trend is useful when the count method and area are unchanged.

activities.title: Inspect leaves and stems for visible damage
activities.why: Early scouting supports timely local diagnosis.

activities.title: Note uneven growth and soil or drainage differences
activities.why: Field variation can explain differing crop development.

name: Vegetative growth
process: Leaf and stalk growth continue, with strong dependence on variety, local season, soil, and water availability.
observations: Measure representative stalk height using the same method
Record tiller or shoot count and sampling area
Note canopy, leaf condition, moisture, and rainfall
frequency: Weekly field scouting; measure height when useful and repeat the same sampling method.

activities.title: Repeat representative height and shoot measurements
activities.why: Consistent measurements create an interpretable history.

activities.title: Review soil moisture, irrigation, and rainfall together
activities.why: A single weather or soil reading is not enough to set irrigation quantities.

activities.title: Review soil-test results and local nutrient schedule
activities.why: Nutrient decisions should use soil tests and region-specific recommendations.

name: Increasing stem growth
process: Stem elongation and internode development may be evident; timing and rate are variety and environment dependent.
observations: Repeat stalk-height measurement on representative plants
Note stem and leaf condition
Record irrigation, rainfall, and any management activity
frequency: Weekly scouting; repeat measurements at consistent intervals and on representative plants.

activities.title: Review height trend and inspect stems
activities.why: The trend plus visual inspection can identify changes that merit investigation.

activities.title: Inspect irrigation coverage and drainage
activities.why: Field-level differences can affect crop condition.

activities.title: Scout for visible pest or disease symptoms
activities.why: Record symptoms and affected plant parts before selecting a response.

name: Six-month crop assessment
process: This checkpoint reviews establishment and early growth evidence. It does not mean the crop is mature or ready to harvest.
observations: Review height and shoot-count history
Summarize leaf and stem condition
Review irrigation, rainfall, soil, and management history
frequency: Complete a checkpoint review near day 180; continue weekly scouting as conditions warrant.

activities.title: Review the first 180 days of recorded crop evidence
activities.why: A checkpoint helps identify unresolved data gaps and follow-up needs.

activities.title: Confirm the next local crop-management window with an extension source
activities.why: Sugarcane commonly grows beyond 180 days and local schedules differ.

activities.title: Carry forward unresolved alerts and tasks
activities.why: Monitoring must continue after the six-month checkpoint.

name: Continued growth and maturity monitoring
process: Continue monitoring after day 180. The system does not infer maturity or harvest readiness from crop age alone.
observations: Continue consistent height, tiller, and crop-condition observations where useful
Record soil moisture, rainfall, irrigation, and symptoms
Use locally verified maturity and harvest indicators
frequency: Weekly scouting or the locally recommended interval; harvest assessment requires regional and variety-specific guidance.

activities.title: Continue crop and symptom scouting
activities.why: Sugarcane duration can extend beyond 180 days.

activities.title: Seek local maturity and harvest-readiness guidance
activities.why: Age alone is insufficient to determine harvest readiness.
